report:
### Conclusion
High-quality clinical evidence demonstrates that **arthroscopy (joint endoscopy) does not provide meaningful or durable benefit for knee osteoarthritis** compared to non-surgical care or placebo.

### Evidence & Recommendations
* **No Superior Benefit Over Placebo or Conservative Care:** Landmark randomized controlled trials published in *The New England Journal of Medicine* established that arthroscopic debridement and lavage offer no significant improvement in pain or physical function over placebo (sham) surgery (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259) or optimized physical therapy and medication (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).
* **Clinical Practice Guidelines:** Major medical bodies advise against the procedure for knee osteoarthritis. A clinical practice guideline in *The BMJ* issued a strong recommendation against arthroscopic knee surgery for degenerative joint disease, noting that any brief pain relief is minimal and offset by surgical risk (https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982). The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) guidelines similarly recommend against routine arthroscopic lavage or debridement for primary knee osteoarthritis (https://new.aaos.org/quality/quality-programs/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/).

**Summary:** Arthroscopy is not recommended as a routine treatment for knee osteoarthritis. First-line management focuses on conservative treatments, including physical therapy, exercise, weight management, and pain medications.

### Sources
* *A Controlled Trial of Arthroscopic Surgery for Osteoarthritis of the Knee* (NEJM): https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259
* *A Randomized Trial of Arthroscopic Surgery for Osteoarthritis of the Knee* (NEJM): https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333
* *BMJ Clinical Practice Guideline:* https://www.bmj.com/content/357/bmj.j1982
* *AAOS Osteoarthritis of the Knee Guidelines:* https://new.aaos.org/quality/quality-programs/osteoarthritis-of-the-knee/
